preamble: In English, the voiceless bilabial stop /p/ is aspirated [pʰ] in syllable-initial position and unaspirated [p] after /s/ or in unstressed syllables. This is a textbook case of allophony: the two phonetic variants are in complementary distribution, conditioned entirely by position within the syllable. English speakers typically do not notice the difference because the aspiration is never phonemically contrastive. Note: in Hindi, Mandarin, and other languages, /p/ and /pʰ/ are distinct phonemes — not allophones — and that contrast is separate from the English allophonic pattern described here. Historically, plain *p became pʰ in Chong (Pearic), as in Proto-Pearic *pliː 'fruit' > pʰliː.

examples.note: 'pit' [pʰɪt] vs. 'spit' [spɪt]: the same phoneme /p/ is aspirated word-initially but unaspirated after /s/. Complementary allophones.
Nguni languages regularly aspirate Proto-Bantu voiceless stops
Pre-Hlai and Proto-Hlai forms are Norquest's (2015) reconstructions as listed in the Wiktionary appendix; the same Initial Aspiration affected *p, *t and *k.
Former *b devoiced without aspiration: Proto-Pearic *bluː 'thigh' > Chong plṳː.

sources: Ladefoged, P., & Maddieson, I. (1996). The Sounds of the World's Languages. Blackwell. https://www.wiley.com/en-us/The+Sounds+of+the+World%27s+Languages-p-9780631198154
Ladefoged, P. (2001). A Course in Phonetics (4th ed.). Harcourt College Publishers. https://lccn.loc.gov/00101369
context: Syllable-initial before stressed vowel = aspirated [pʰ]; post-/s/ = unaspirated [p]
